papers.title: Using waveform types, discrete Sobolev distances, and trend compatibility to cluster short time series of clinical data
papers.label: arXiv:2611.33623v1

summary.one_liner: A nonparametric method that groups short, undersampled clinical response curves (five-point oral glucose tolerance tests) by sorting them into trend-compatible unit waveforms and comparing shapes with discrete Sobolev-type distances, with the number of clusters set by the trend patterns the cohort actually populates.
summary.plain: Clinical tests such as the glucose tolerance test push the body out of rest and record how glucose and insulin change over a few timed blood samples. The paper proposes a way to group these very short curves by their overall shape, so that patients who recover from the test in similar ways end up together. Applied to 1283 tests, it found 7 glycemia response types and 8 insulin response types, and it kept the same count across a threefold range of resolution.
summary.why: Short clinical curves usually get reduced to a few summary numbers, which discards how the body recovers after the challenge; this paper offers a way to keep that trend information. The text reports benchmarks against six classical clustering methods, where the proposed method alone never mixed opposite trends, but it does not establish clinical usefulness, and the link to diagnosis is only suggested by the graded clinical-normality result.
summary.background:
- Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT): a patient drinks a sugar solution and blood glucose and insulin are measured at a few times afterward.
- Time series: a sequence of measurements over time; "undersampled" means only a few points are taken.
- Clustering: grouping items so that members of a group are similar and different groups are distinct.
- Finite differences: changes between neighbouring points; the order k indicates how many times you take differences, capturing trend and curvature.
- Sobolev-type distance: a way of measuring how different two curves are, including how their slopes and bends differ, not just their heights.
- Resampling validation: checking that a result holds when the data are randomly re-drawn or re-split.
- Nonparametric: makes few assumptions about the shape of the underlying data distribution.

papers.abstract: Clinical tests, such as the oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), perturb a physiological system at rest and record its excursion over a fixed protocol window as a short, undersampled time series. Such curves rarely allow parameter identification at the individual level, yet their trends carry physiological information that emerges at the population level as recurrent response patterns. Standard clustering methods aggregate differences globally and average out those trends, losing precisely the information about how the system regains control after the perturbation; identifying response patterns requires a method that preserves them. We present a nonparametric framework that factorizes each curve into unit waveforms, sorts them with a symbolic trend-compatibility filter, and compares compatible shapes using discrete Sobolev-type distances on finite differences up to order $k$. The number of clusters, i.e., distinct response types, equals the number of realizable trend patterns the cohort populates, validated by resampling. Applied to 1283 five-point OGTTs, the method identifies 7 glycemia and 8 insulinemia types. The count holds across a threefold range of resolution. In benchmarks against six classical clustering methods, ours alone never mixes opposite trends, with comparable reconstruction error and stability. Clinical normality, assessed after clustering, is graded, overlapping, and distributed unevenly across response types ($h=0.14$--$0.48$). Overall, our method distinguishes response types among curves too short for alignment-based methods yet too informative for reduction to summary values. It applies to any protocol recording a system's response to a standardized perturbation on a short grid.

papers.title: k-Nearest Neighbors estimation of the drift of an ergodic diffusion process under Osgood regularity
papers.label: arXiv:2611.33596v1

summary.one_liner: The paper proves consistency of k-nearest-neighbors estimators for the drift (deterministic trend) of an ergodic diffusion process over compact and non-compact intervals, under relatively weak regularity (Osgood-type) conditions on the coefficients.
summary.plain: The paper studies how to estimate the hidden "pull" that shapes a randomly moving process, such as a noisy price or particle path that keeps returning to a typical range. The authors apply the k-nearest-neighbors method, a simple idea that averages nearby observations, and show it converges to the true answer under fairly mild assumptions. Previous work on this approach had mostly relied on computer experiments rather than proofs.
summary.why: Putting a mathematical guarantee behind a popular, easy-to-use method extends the justification for using it in the statistics of continuous-time random processes. The text does not indicate applications beyond the numerical illustrations it mentions, so wider impact is unclear.
summary.background:
- Diffusion process: a continuous random motion, described by a drift (average direction of movement) and a volatility (size of random noise).
- Ergodic: the process over time explores its typical states, so long observations reveal its long-run behaviour.
- Drift estimation: inferring the drift function from observed trajectory data.
- k-nearest neighbors (kNN): estimating a value at a point by averaging the k observations closest to it.
- Consistency: the estimator converges to the true function as the amount of data grows.
- Osgood regularity: a mild smoothness condition on the coefficients, weaker than the usual differentiability assumptions.
- Compact vs non-compact interval: whether the state range is bounded or extends without limit.

papers.abstract: The k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN) algorithm is a widely used machine learning method with well-established theoretical guarantees for consistent estimation in multivariate settings and functional time series analysis. In the context of nonparametric estimation of the coefficients of ergodic diffusion processes, however, its use has so far been mainly illustrated through numerical experiments. The main contribution of this paper is to establish theoretical consistency results for drift kNN estimators over both compact and non-compact intervals, under relatively weak regularity conditions on the coefficients of the underlying ergodic diffusion process. The theoretical results are completed with numerical illustrations.

papers.title: Design-based causal inference for ROC curves
papers.label: arXiv:2611.34057v1

summary.background:
- Randomized experiment: people are randomly assigned to treatment or control, so the groups are comparable on average.
- Potential outcomes: each person has an outcome under treatment and one under control; only one is observed.
- Design-based inference: uncertainty comes from the random assignment itself, not from assuming a statistical model for outcomes.
- ROC curve: originally from diagnostic testing, it plots the true-positive rate against the false-positive rate; here it is used to compare two outcome distributions.
- Quantile: the value below which a given share of a group falls (e.g., the 90th percentile is the score exceeded by 10% of the group).
- Covariate adjustment: using pre-treatment background variables to sharpen estimates.
- Confidence band: a range around a whole curve, not just a single point, that is expected to contain the true curve with a stated probability.
summary.one_liner: A design-based framework for estimating the ROC curve, which compares treated and control outcome distributions in randomized experiments, with rank-based estimation, covariate adjustment, simultaneous confidence bands, and extreme-tail inference.
summary.plain: This paper is about comparing how a treatment changes the whole spread of outcomes, not just the average. Instead of asking only whether the treated group does better on average, it asks, for each cutoff level in the control group, what share of treated people score above that cutoff. The authors build an estimator from pooled ranks of the outcomes, prove it behaves well for large samples, and show how to attach confidence intervals to it.
summary.why: Many experiments care about who gains, not only the average gain, and this gives a way to study that without assuming a specific model of the outcomes. The text also reports that covariate adjustment can reduce variance and that the methods are tested on a large online learning experiment, though the text gives no further detail on how much improvement that yields.

papers.abstract: In randomized experiments, causal inference traditionally focuses on the average treatment effect, yet comparing the treatment and control potential outcome distributions is often of interest. Under complete randomization, we adopt a design-based framework without imposing an outcome model to study the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, which measures the proportion of treated outcomes exceeding each upper quantile of the control distribution. We propose an estimator that depends only on pooled outcome ranks, establish its asymptotic normality, and construct conservative variance estimators and confidence intervals. We also develop covariate adjustment directly for the ROC estimator, preserving the target estimand while achieving an asymptotic variance no larger than that of the unadjusted estimator. We further construct simultaneous confidence bands over an interior range of quantile levels and extend pointwise inference to the extreme upper tail of the control distribution, with both extensions accommodating covariate adjustment. Simulation studies and an application to a large-scale online learning experiment illustrate the proposed methods.

papers.title: BADGERS: Bayesian Adaptive Graph-Guided Errors-in-Variables Regression Solution for Structured High-Dimensional Data
papers.label: arXiv:2611.34378v1

summary.background:
- High-dimensional data: many more measured variables (e.g., thousands of genes) than samples.
- Errors-in-variables: when predictors are measured with noise, naive regression gives biased results.
- Latent variables: unobserved "true" values inferred from noisy measurements.
- Bayesian methods: combine prior beliefs with data to get a distribution over possible answers; Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) is a sampling method used to compute these.
- Graphical lasso: a technique that estimates how variables are linked, encouraging sparse (few-connection) networks.
- Shrinkage priors: settings that pull weak effects toward zero to select variables.
- Omics: large-scale biological measurement fields such as genomics and transcriptomics.
summary.one_liner: BADGERS is a Bayesian regression framework that handles measurement error in replicated high-dimensional covariates (such as gene expression) while using a biological graph to guide variable selection and model the dependence among covariates.
summary.plain: Many gene studies measure the same quantity several times because each measurement is noisy, and standard analysis tools usually ignore that noise. This paper proposes a statistical method, BADGERS, that estimates the underlying "true" values from the repeated readings, uses a known biological network of related genes to help decide which genes matter, and tests the approach on simulated data and on gene expression datasets for Alzheimer's disease and multiple myeloma. The summary text reports advantages over existing methods in simulations and real-data analyses, but it does not give the specific numbers.
summary.why: Ignoring measurement error can bias which variables appear important, and omics studies often have this problem, so a method that accounts for it while using biological network information may be useful. Its practical value depends on details (such as computational cost and performance across settings) that the summary does not report.

papers.abstract: Knowledge-guided learning methods that incorporate biological graph information into the analysis of structured high-dimensional data, such as genomic data, can improve variable selection and prediction accuracy while yielding more interpretable results. However, these methods typically assume that covariates are measured without error. This assumption is often violated in omics studies involving replicated measurements. To address this gap, we develop the Bayesian Adaptive Graph-guided Errors-in-variables Regression Solution (BADGERS), a Bayesian framework that jointly accounts for covariate measurement error and incorporates graph information while accommodating varying numbers of replicates across covariates. BADGERS treats the true covariates as latent variables and integrates three key components: a Gaussian errors-in-variables model using replicated measurements to inform the latent true covariates, a Bayesian adaptive graphical lasso with a graph-informed prior to model their dependence structure, and a regression model with an adaptive structured shrinkage prior to leverage graph information and facilitate variable selection. We develop an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm for posterior sampling. We demonstrate the advantages of BADGERS over existing methods through simulation studies and analyses of gene expression datasets for Alzheimer's disease and multiple myeloma.

papers.title: Admissibility of Linear Time Series Models under Cone Constraints
papers.label: arXiv:2611.32414v1

summary.background:
- Stationary time series: a process whose statistical behaviour does not change over time.
- Linear process: each value is a weighted sum of current and past random shocks (innovations).
- Hilbert space: an infinite-dimensional vector space, used here so that functions such as densities or quantile curves can be treated as data points.
- Closed convex cone: a set closed under addition and non-negative scaling, such as non-negative functions or positive semidefinite matrices; the "largest linear subspace" inside it is the part where the cone's constraints act like ordinary equalities.
- Almost surely: holding with probability one.
- Fractional filter: a weighting scheme with slowly decaying coefficients, giving long-memory behaviour.
- Quantile function: the inverse of a cumulative distribution function, describing the spread of a distribution.
- Mean square boundedness: the average squared size of a quantity stays finite over time.
summary.one_liner: The paper gives a necessary and sufficient support condition for stationary Hilbert-space linear processes to stay almost surely inside a closed convex cone, and studies what this implies for additive linear models of quantiles, densities and covariance operators.
summary.plain: Many data objects, such as probability densities, quantile curves and covariance matrices, must obey built-in rules (for example, being non-negative or increasing). The paper asks when the usual additive way of modelling a series over time, where each value is a weighted sum of past random shocks, can respect those rules. It finds that with certain shock distributions, including Gaussian ones, the randomness is forced into a restricted subspace, and it constructs working models that avoid this for quantiles, densities and covariance matrices.
summary.why: Standard linear time series models are widely used, so knowing exactly when they remain valid for constrained objects matters for applied modelling of distributions and covariances. The text is a theoretical abstract, so its practical reach beyond these model classes is not shown here.

papers.abstract: Time series analysis extends beyond vector-valued observations to evolving probability densities, quantile functions, and covariance operators. These objects carry intrinsic constraints, raising questions about the admissibility of additive linear models, which have long served as a foundation for time series modelling and theory. We give a necessary and sufficient support condition for a stationary Hilbert-space linear process to remain in a closed convex cone almost surely. Innovations with unbounded lower tails, including Gaussian innovations, confine randomness to the cone's largest linear subspace. For fractional filters with convergent normalized cumulative coefficients, the leading stochastic directions obey the same restriction, even with bounded innovations. For real-line quantiles, variation under unbounded lower tails and leading fractional accumulation can occur only through location shifts. For cone-valued processes, partial sums of centred stationary increments remain bounded in mean square when evaluated by any linear functional that is nonnegative on the cone, in contrast to the growing variance of a random walk. We derive an exact slope criterion for locally absolutely continuous quantiles and construct nondegenerate additive models with bounded innovations for quantiles, densities, and covariance matrices. These findings clarify the scope of ordinary additive modelling under structural constraints.

papers.title: Exact local queries for pseudo-marginal Markov chains
papers.label: arXiv:2611.32955v1

summary.background:
- Markov chain: a sequence of random states where each new state depends on the previous one.
- Pseudo-marginal sampling: a Monte Carlo method where an estimate of a likelihood (how well data fit a setting) replaces its exact value, while still targeting the correct distribution.
- Gaussian graph prior: a probability model over parameters attached to nodes of a network (graph), where neighbouring nodes are linked.
- Auxiliary variables: extra randomly introduced variables that make sampling easier.
- Picard iteration: a method that repeatedly refines a guess until it stops changing, used here as a comparison.
- Gaussian process classification: a method that learns a flexible function to sort data into classes.
- Positron emission tomography (PET): an imaging method that reconstructs a spatial map from detected emissions.
- Monte Carlo uncertainty: the error that comes from using finite random samples.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes "decision certificates" built from finite historical parameter ranges that let a pseudo-marginal Markov chain on Gaussian graph priors answer prespecified local queries exactly, without resolving all neighbouring updates first, and reports work bounds and experiments on path/grid graphs and two applications.
summary.plain: Markov chain samplers are computer procedures that wander through possible parameter settings to approximate a probability distribution, and often each step depends on earlier steps. This paper looks at how to read off the value of one part of such a chain on demand, without recomputing everything that came before. The authors report that, under their stated assumptions, this selective method recovers the same results as the full computation while doing less work for sparse requests, though full requests were faster with the alternative method.
summary.why: It targets a practical cost problem in Bayesian computation, namely how much work is needed to query one piece of a long sampling chain, and it tests the idea on tomography and classification examples. The text does not show how broadly the approach would transfer beyond the stated graph families and models.

papers.abstract: Local queries of a Markov chain can depend on past updates outside the queried components. For pseudo-marginal chains with Gaussian graph priors, we construct decision certificates from finite historical parameter ranges to settle updates before all neighbouring records are resolved. Under shared random inputs and exact arithmetic, the executor recovers the reference parameters, auxiliary variables and likelihood estimates for any prespecified finite query sequence. We bound conditional expected work, including likelihood evaluation, historical range construction and execution management. On specified path and grid families, we fix per-node history lengths and all other parameters in the work bounds. As graph size grows, expected incremental work stays bounded for certificate execution and grows linearly for the specified cached pointwise evaluator answering the same query. In controlled experiments, certificate execution is faster than pointwise and parallel Picard execution for sparse queries, whereas Picard is faster than certificate execution for full queries. We apply the method to positron emission tomography and Gaussian process classification of Landmine data. For a fixed numerical tomography posterior, certificate execution completes all queries of regional mean distribution volume within budget, while full execution completes none from the same initial cache. In Landmine, posterior summaries of the difference in log length scales between two sites agree across pseudo-marginal and ancillary augmentation samplers within estimated Monte Carlo uncertainty. Certificate execution resolves almost every scheduled update over the full query sequence.

papers.title: Targeted Learning for Externally Controlled Trials and Beyond
papers.label: arXiv:2611.28421v1

summary.background:
- Externally controlled trial: a single-group trial whose control comparison comes from outside the trial (old trial, cohort study, or real-world data).
- Estimand: the precise quantity being estimated, such as an average treatment effect in a defined population.
- Balancing weights: numerical weights given to patients in the external group so that their covariates resemble those of the trial group.
- Efficient influence function: a mathematical object that describes how precisely an estimate can be made, used to derive the best-possible estimator.
- Targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE): a two-step method that first models outcomes, then nudges them to reduce bias for the target quantity.
- Individual patient data (IPD) vs aggregate data (AgD): row-level records versus summary statistics published for a group.
- Indirect treatment comparison: comparing two treatments that were never tested head-to-head, via a common comparator.
summary.one_liner: The paper develops efficient influence function and targeted maximum likelihood estimators for a class of balancing-weight estimands in externally controlled trials, with extensions to trials augmented by external covariate data and to indirect treatment comparisons using individual and aggregate patient data.
summary.plain: When a new drug is tested in a single group of patients, researchers sometimes compare it with a control group drawn from older trials, patient registries, or real-world records instead of randomizing a concurrent control. This paper gives a statistical recipe for estimating the treatment effect in that setting while adjusting for differences between the two groups. The authors describe a method that is designed to be more reliable in finite samples, and they also show how the same approach can be applied to two related situations.
summary.why: Externally controlled trials are used when randomization is hard or unethical, so better-justified estimators matter for regulatory and medical decisions. The text does not report empirical results or comparisons, so its practical benefit beyond the stated theoretical properties cannot be judged from this summary alone.

papers.abstract: This paper focuses on externally controlled trials (ECTs), which consist of a single-arm clinical trial supplemented by an external control arm (ECA). Potential data sources for the ECA can be broadly classified into three categories: (i) the control arm of a historical clinical trial, (ii) a concurrent cohort study, and (iii) external real-world data (RWD). In this paper, we consider a broad class of estimands defined through balancing weights. For a given estimand in the class, we discuss the efficient influence function (EIF) and the targeted maximum likelihood estimator (TMLE), together with practical implementation algorithms. Within the targeted learning framework, TMLE is a substitution estimator that enjoys several desirable theoretical properties and favorable finite-sample performance. Finally, the proposed framework is extended to two additional settings: (1) randomized controlled trials (RCTs) augmented with external covariate information to define a target population, and (2) indirect treatment comparisons (ITCs) that combine individual patient data (IPD) from an internal RCT with aggregate data (AgD) from an external RCT.

papers.title: Threshold Generalized Autoregressive Moving Average Models
papers.label: arXiv:2611.28271v1

summary.background:
- Time series: data recorded in order over time, where past values help predict future ones.
- Non-Gaussian data: outcomes that are not bell-curve shaped, such as counts of events.
- GARMA models: extensions of ARMA models that handle non-normal outcomes by linking the mean to past observations and past errors.
- Threshold models: models that use different sets of rules depending on whether a variable is above or below a cutoff (the threshold).
- Partial likelihood: a way of estimating parameters when a full probability model is hard to specify completely.
- Information criteria (such as AIC or BIC): scores that balance model fit against complexity to choose among models.
- Mean squared error: the average squared gap between predicted and observed values; lower is better.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes threshold GARMA models, an observation-driven extension of generalized autoregressive moving-average models for non-Gaussian time series that switch between regimes based on a lagged threshold variable, with partial-likelihood estimation, information-criterion model selection, and an application to monthly respiratory hospitalization counts in São Paulo.
summary.plain: Many real-world counts, such as monthly hospital admissions, do not follow a simple steady pattern and can behave differently depending on the situation, for example in high versus low periods. This paper builds a statistical model that lets the rules governing the data switch between regimes depending on a past value of a chosen variable. The authors test it on monthly respiratory hospitalizations among older adults in São Paulo, Brazil, and report that it fits better in-sample than the single-regime version, measured by mean squared error.
summary.why: Count data with changing behavior are common in health and environmental monitoring, so a model that allows regime-dependent dynamics may be useful there. The evidence shown is limited to one application and in-sample error, so its value for forecasting or other datasets is not established by this text alone.

papers.abstract: Non-Gaussian time series often exhibit nonlinear dynamics and changes in dependence structures that may not be adequately captured by conventional single-regime models. To address this limitation, we introduce a class of threshold generalized autoregressive moving-average (TGARMA) models that combines observation-driven GARMA dynamics with threshold-based regime switching. The proposed framework accommodates multiple regimes, determined by a lagged endogenous or exogenous threshold variable, and allows regression coefficients, autoregressive and moving-average orders and coefficients, and, where applicable, dispersion parameters to vary across regimes. Parameters are estimated by maximum partial likelihood, while model selection is conducted using information criteria. We examine model admissibility and stability, assess model adequacy through residual diagnostics, and conduct a Monte Carlo simulation study to investigate the finite-sample performance of the estimators. The proposed methodology is illustrated using monthly counts of hospitalizations due to respiratory diseases among older adults in S\~ao Paulo, Brazil. In this application, the TGARMA model outperforms its single-regime GARMA counterpart in terms of in-sample mean squared error, highlighting the potential benefits of incorporating regime-dependent dynamics into the analysis of non-Gaussian time series.

papers.title: Hidden Semi-Markov Models for Fully Functional Time Series
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26838v1

summary.background:
- Hidden Markov model: a model where an unseen state changes over time, and each state produces the observed data.
- Markov property: the next state depends only on the current one, which makes durations decay geometrically.
- Semi-Markov / sojourn time: a model that lets the time spent in a state follow its own distribution, such as a negative binomial.
- Baum-Welch and Viterbi: standard algorithms for fitting such models and finding the most likely hidden state sequence.
- Functional time series: data where each observation is a whole curve or function, not a single number.
- Gaussian measures on locally convex spaces: a generalization of normal distributions to infinite-dimensional settings, used here to handle curves.
- EEG and polysomnography: recordings of brain electrical activity and other signals during sleep.
summary.one_liner: The paper extends hidden semi-Markov models, with data-driven state durations, to fully functional time series, embedding the hidden chain in a larger Markov chain so Baum-Welch and Viterbi fitting can be used, and applies this to pediatric EEG signals in the Gaussian-measure setting of locally convex spaces.
summary.plain: Many signals, such as brain recordings, switch between hidden modes over time, and a common model for this is the hidden Markov model. That model forces each mode to last for a random time that drops off quickly, which often does not fit real data. This paper replaces it with a version where each hidden mode can last for a more flexible, data-driven length, and applies the approach to overnight sleep-study EEG recordings from children.
summary.why: Modeling how long a hidden state lasts is central to interpreting physiological signals such as sleep stages, so a more realistic duration model may matter for that kind of analysis. The provided text does not report comparative results against standard models, so its practical gain is not established here.

papers.abstract: Functional time series have a wide range of practical applications to modeling complex datasets such as Electroencephalogram (EEG) and other biological signals. Often latent states are hidden within the data dictating how a system is behaving and changing over time. The Hidden Markov Model (HMM) is one common and highly applicable latent state space model where the hidden state sequence evolves as a Markov chain. While the HMM has had much success modeling discrete, multivariate, and fully functional time series, it is also restricted by the Markov property which causes hidden states to persist only at geometrically decaying rates. This work investigates the implementation of hidden semi-Markov models for modeling fully functional time series data. This allows for the hidden state sequence to persist in a given state for a data-driven sojourn time, which can be parametrized by a discrete distribution (e.g. negative binomial) or left non-parametric. For efficient fitting of such a model, the hidden semi-Markov chain is embedded into a larger state space Markov chain and classic methods like the Baum-Welch and Viterbi algorithms are applied. We furthermore consider functional time series in the general setting of Gaussian measures in locally convex topological vector spaces. This is applied to a time series of pediatric EEG signals collected via overnight polysomnography.

papers.title: A generalized Bayesian method for identifying local and global changepoints in dynamic network data
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26955v1

summary.background:
- A dynamic network is a sequence of snapshots over time, each recorded as an adjacency matrix (a grid where an entry marks whether two nodes are linked).
- A changepoint is a time at which the underlying process generating the data shifts.
- Bayesian inference combines a prior belief with observed data to get a posterior distribution, which expresses uncertainty about unknown quantities.
- A generalized posterior replaces the usual likelihood with a loss function, so the method does not depend on knowing the exact data-generating process.
- Low-rank structure and sparsity are simplifying assumptions that keep the model parameters compact and mostly zero.
- Gibbs sampling and Pólya-Gamma data augmentation are computational techniques for drawing samples from the posterior.
summary.one_liner: A generalized Bayesian changepoint method for dynamic networks uses a multinomial log loss, a low-rank sparse prior, and a Pólya-Gamma Gibbs sampler to locate local and global structural shifts in time-indexed adjacency matrices.
summary.plain: The paper addresses how to find the moments when a network that changes over time (such as who emails whom, or which countries are in conflict) suddenly shifts its pattern. The authors build a statistical method that looks at both the full set of connections and simple summary measures of the network, and it estimates where the change points are along with how uncertain those estimates are. They report that in simulations it was often more accurate than competing methods, and they illustrate it on an email network and an international conflict network.
summary.why: Detecting when relationships in a network change matters for fields that track communication, social ties, or political conflict over time. The text does not say how broadly the method will transfer beyond the benchmark simulations and the two applications shown.

papers.abstract: We introduce a generalized Bayesian approach to multiple changepoint analysis in dynamic network data based on a multinomial log loss function and a prior distribution that imposes low-rank structure and sparsity on the model parameters. The method can detect local and global changes in network structure by incorporating information from both the full adjacency matrices and network summary statistics. Moreover, the proposed method is agnostic to the true data-generating process. From the generalized posterior distribution, we can make simultaneous inferences with meaningful uncertainty quantification about the locations of changepoints as well as deduce the network attributes and summary statistics that characterize them. For posterior simulation, we develop an efficient Gibbs sampler based on P\'olya-Gamma data augmentation with a computational cost that grows linearly with the number of observed edges in the dynamic network. Simulations across several benchmark network models show that the proposed method is often more accurate and flexible than competitors. We demonstrate the practical value of the method through applications to an email communication network and an international conflict network.

papers.title: Faithful Generative Modeling for Censored Time-to-Event Data: From Distributional Fidelity to Statistical Inference
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25464v1

summary.background:
- Time-to-event (survival) data: measurements of how long until something happens, such as relapse or death.
- Censoring: some subjects are not followed until the event, so only a lower bound on their time is known.
- Cox proportional hazards model: a standard regression model that relates covariates to the risk of an event over time.
- Generative model: a method that learns a data distribution and produces new samples resembling it.
- Distributional fidelity: how closely synthetic data follow the statistical pattern of real data.
- Consistency and variance correction: an estimator is consistent if it converges to the true value with more data; variance correction adjusts estimated uncertainty so confidence statements are valid.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes a two-stage generative model (TSGSurv) for synthetic censored time-to-event data, proves a distributional convergence rate for it, and studies when Cox proportional hazards inference on synthetic survival data is valid and how to correct it.
summary.plain: The paper is about creating artificial patient records that mimic real survival data, meaning how long until an event such as death or relapse happens, where some cases are only partly observed (censored). The authors build a two-step generator that produces observed times and covariates together, and they claim theoretical guarantees on how closely the fake data match the real distribution. They also show that standard statistical analysis run on synthetic data can be misleading, and they describe a variance correction and a distribution calibration step to recover valid conclusions about the original data.
summary.why: Synthetic patient data is increasingly used for data sharing, trial simulation and digital twins, so whether analyses on such data are trustworthy matters for medical research. The text does not say how the methods compare with existing approaches beyond the reported simulations and two real-data applications, so its practical reach is uncertain from the abstract alone.

papers.abstract: Synthetic data has emerged as a powerful tool for data sharing, clinical trial simulation, and digital twin development, with growing applications in biomedical research and drug development. However, limited attention has been devoted to synthetic time-to-event data, which are central to clinical trials and survival analysis. In particular, theoretical guarantees for the distributional fidelity of synthetic survival data remain largely unexplored. More importantly, even when a generator achieves distributional fidelity, it remains unclear whether the downstream statistical analysis is reliable. To address these gaps, we propose a general two-stage generative framework for survival data (TSGSurv) that jointly generates observed times and covariates conditional on event status, and establish its distributional convergence rate. Focusing on the widely used Cox proportional hazards model, we establish conditions under which generator fidelity guarantees consistency of model coefficient estimates. We further characterize the limitations of naive inference based on synthetic data, and develop a variance correction and a distribution calibration procedure to recover valid inference of original data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed generative and inferential framework with extensive simulations and two real data applications.

papers.title: Exact Bayesian layers via characteristic functions
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26426v1

summary.background:
- Bayesian neural network: a neural network whose weights are uncertain, so predictions come with uncertainty estimates.
- Variational inference: training by fitting a simpler approximate distribution, optimizing a score called the evidence lower bound (ELBO).
- Monte Carlo sampling: estimating quantities by averaging many random draws; accurate but costly.
- Sampling-free propagation: computing how uncertainty moves through a layer analytically instead of by drawing samples.
- ReLU: a common layer function that outputs zero for negative inputs and the input itself otherwise.
- Characteristic function: a mathematical transform that uniquely describes a probability distribution, similar in role to a fingerprint.
- Likelihood: the assumed probability model for the observed data (e.g., Gaussian, Poisson, Gamma).
- Calibration error: how far a model's stated confidence differs from how often it is actually right.
summary.one_liner: CF-Prop propagates characteristic functions through a Bayesian ReLU layer to get the exact output distribution without sampling, enabling a closed-form evidence lower bound for non-Gaussian likelihoods (CF-VI).
summary.plain: Bayesian neural networks give predictions with honest uncertainty, but estimating that uncertainty usually means running many random samples, which is slow. This paper proposes a way to track the full shape of the uncertainty through a network layer directly, without sampling, and to train with it even when the data are not bell-shaped, such as counts or heavy-tailed insurance claims.
summary.why: Many sampling-free methods assume the output uncertainty is Gaussian, which the authors note can be inaccurate in applied problems. The reported results (lowest calibration error on CIFAR-100, and better capture of tail uncertainty on an insurance claims dataset) suggest the approach may matter for applied uncertainty estimation, though the text alone does not show how broadly it generalizes.

papers.abstract: Bayesian neural networks provide principled uncertainty estimates, but training them with Monte Carlo sampling can be expensive. Sampling-free variational inference algorithms make training Bayesian neural networks feasible, but existing approaches assume a Gaussian output distribution, which can be inaccurate in applied problems. Here, we introduce CF-Prop, an uncertainty propagation method that uses characteristic functions to compute the exact output distribution of a Bayesian ReLU layer, without any sampling, even in non-Gaussian settings. Because CF-Prop propagates characteristic functions, the evidence lower bound---the objective of variational training---can be computed in closed form for a broad class of likelihoods, including the Gaussian, Poisson, and Gamma. This allows to implement an efficient resulting variational inference algorithm, CF-VI. On CIFAR-100, CF-VI achieves the lowest calibration error of any tested method, improving on the next best method by about 35%. On a heavy-tailed insurance claim dataset, CF-VI accurately captures tail uncertainty that is severely underestimated by both other sampling-free methods and Monte Carlo methods.

papers.title: Fill-Distance-Guided Active Learning for Causal Function Recovery under Network Interference
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24143v1

summary.background:
- Causal inference: estimating how outcomes would change under different interventions.
- Network interference (spillovers): one unit's outcome depends on others' treatments, so the treatment effect depends on the neighborhood exposure pattern.
- Response function: the curve or surface giving the average outcome for each exposure pattern.
- Active learning: choosing the next data points adaptively to learn a function efficiently under a limited budget.
- Gaussian processes: flexible statistical models for unknown nonlinear functions that also give uncertainty estimates.
- Fill distance: a measure of the largest gap between data points in a space; small fill distance means the space is well covered.
- Uniform error bounds: guarantees on estimation error holding across the whole domain, not only at selected points.
summary.one_liner: FANCI uses fill-distance-guided active learning with treatment-specific Gaussian processes to recover the full exposure-dependent population-average response function under network interference, with uniform error bounds and a target-screening approximation analysis.
summary.plain: When people in a network influence each other, one person's outcome depends on their own treatment and on their neighbors' treatments. This paper asks how to run a limited number of experiments so that the whole curve of outcomes across these neighborhood exposure patterns can be learned, rather than just one or two comparisons. The authors propose a method that chooses new experiments in regions where the data is sparse, and they report simulations and an online-game experiment where it recovers nonlinear effects better.
summary.why: Most causal methods focus on specific contrasts or on how precisely they are estimated, so learning the whole response shape under interference is a less-explored goal. The approach may be relevant to platform experiments, public health, and social-network interventions, though the text alone does not show how broadly it transfers.

papers.abstract: Causal inference seeks to learn how outcomes change under alternative interventions, but network interactions complicate this task. Under network interference, outcomes depend on both own treatment and neighbors' treatments, making causal effects functions of neighborhood exposure rather than single treatment contrasts. Existing methods primarily target prespecified causal contrasts or their estimation precision, leaving global response-function recovery largely unexplored. We study sequential experimentation under a limited experimental budget, with the goal of recovering the full exposure-dependent population-average response function. To this end, we propose FANCI (Fill-Distance-Guided Active Learning for Network-Interference Causal Inference). For function learning, treatment-specific Gaussian processes flexibly model nonlinear conditional response surfaces. For experimental design, we formulate global response-function recovery as a coverage problem and propose a fill-distance criterion that guides new experiments toward poorly covered regions. To account for network constraints on attainable exposure patterns, we develop full-network and target-screened strategies for selecting feasible network--assignment pairs. Theoretically, we derive uniform error bounds linking fill distance to response-function estimation and characterize the approximation loss from target screening. Simulations and an online-game experiment show that FANCI improves recovery of nonlinear exposure-dependent effects and reveals treatment patterns obscured when network interference is ignored.

papers.title: Global sensitivity analysis of transient regimes in non-Newtonian dam-break flows applied in rheometry
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24335v1

summary.background:
- Non-Newtonian fluid: a material whose resistance to flow changes with how it is pushed (e.g., paste, concrete, some foods), unlike water.
- Dam-break flow: what happens when a retaining barrier is removed and the fluid collapses and spreads.
- Rheometry: the measurement of how a material flows and deforms.
- Yield stress: the minimum push needed before the material starts to flow.
- Slump test / Bostwick consistometer: simple empirical tests that measure how far a sample spreads under its own weight.
- Global sensitivity analysis: a statistical way to rank how much each input variable contributes to output variation across its full range; here adapted to outputs that change over time.
- High-fidelity simulation: detailed computer modelling, here done with ANSYS Fluent software.
summary.one_liner: A global sensitivity analysis adapted for time-series outputs, applied to ANSYS Fluent simulations, that maps how lifting velocity, viscosity and initial sample geometry influence the time-evolving dynamics of non-Newtonian dam-break flows used in rheometry.
summary.plain: When a container holding a thick, paste-like material is lifted, the material spreads out, and how it spreads depends on how fast the container is lifted and on the material's properties. This paper uses computer simulations of that spreading and a statistical method to measure how much each input (mainly lifting speed) matters at different stages. It finds three phases, and the lifting speed matters most in the first two.
summary.why: Simple field tests such as the slump test and Bostwick consistometer test estimate a material's flow properties from how it spreads, so unwanted effects from lifting the container could bias those estimates. The paper's time-resolved sensitivity curves give a way to see when those effects matter, though the text itself does not report how far the findings transfer to real test equipment.

papers.abstract: Non-Newtonian dam-break flows are a classical problem with numerous engineering applications. These flows are particularly important in alternative rheometry, where they are used to rapidly and affordably estimate rheological properties, such as in the slump test and Bostwick consistometer test. However, the lifting dynamics of the containing obstacle introduce inertial effects that can compromise the accurate estimation of these properties. These effects are influenced by the lifting velocity, the fluid's viscosity, and the initial geometry of the sample. This study aims to quantify the influence of lifting velocity and to provide physical insights into how inertial effects influence the flow. A global sensitivity analysis (GSA) framework adapted for functional outputs (e.g., time series) is employed, using data generated from high-fidelity simulations with ANSYS Fluent. The GSA produces sensitivity curves that track the evolving importance of each input parameter over time. Three distinct flow regimes are identified, namely mobilization, transition and viscous regimes, each governed by different dominant factors. The first two regimes are significantly affected by the lifting velocity, revealing the influence of inertial effects, whereas the viscous regime is dominated by fluid rheology and shows a increasing importance of the yield stress. These results are contextualized in terms of traditional rheometry tests.

papers.title: Small Area Causal Inference
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22339v1

summary.background:
- Causal inference: estimating what would have happened to the same units with and without a treatment.
- Small area estimation: producing reliable estimates for subgroups (regions, farms, clinics) that have few observations.
- Doubly robust (DR) estimation: a standard causal method that stays valid if either of two underlying models is correctly specified; it is mainly judged by bias.
- Linear mixed model: a regression model with fixed effects plus random effects that let each area borrow strength from the others.
- Empirical best prediction (EBP): predicting an area's value using estimated model parameters, chosen to minimise expected squared prediction error.
- Mean squared prediction error (MSPE): the average squared gap between prediction and truth; lower is better.
- Asymptotic results (consistency, normality, optimality): statements about how estimators behave as sample size grows large, not guarantees for small samples.
- Prediction interval and coverage: a range meant to contain the true value, and the share of cases where it actually does.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes an empirical best prediction (EBP) framework for estimating area-specific causal effects in small areas, using a linear mixed model, with theory on estimator consistency, asymptotic normality, MSPE optimality, and prediction intervals, compared against doubly robust estimation in simulations and a real agricultural-genetics example.
summary.plain: The paper looks at how to estimate the effect of a treatment or intervention separately for small geographic or group areas, where there are only a few observations per area. The authors propose a method, called empirical best prediction, that balances bias against the noise in small samples rather than focusing mainly on bias as the traditional doubly robust approach does. In their simulations it gave more accurate predictions and prediction intervals with better coverage than the comparison methods, and they also apply it to a farm-animal genetics dataset.
summary.why: Estimating causal effects for small subgroups is hard because each subgroup has little data, so noise often dominates error. The paper's claim that variance, not just bias, drives most of the error is a reasonable point for small-area work, but the advantage is shown only in the authors' simulations and one real example, so its broader practical reach is not yet established.

papers.abstract: We develop a framework for small area causal inference (SACI). Unlike the traditional doubly robust (DR) estimation approach, the new framework is based on the empirical best prediction (EBP) method. EBP takes into consideration not only the bias but also the variance factor, which is often a more dominant component in the mean squared prediction error (MSPE). Under a linear mixed model for SACI, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the maximum likelihood estimator of the model parameters. More relevant to our main objective, we establish asymptotic optimality of the EBP in terms of minimizing the MSPE of the area-specific causal-effect (ASCE) predictor. Moreover, in view of the traditional interest in causal inference, we establish asymptotic normality of the EBP of the ASCE , which is used to construct prediction intervals for the ASCEs. We carry out extensive simulation studies to investigate finite-sample performance of the proposed EBP and its comparison with the traditional DR and other existing methods. Our simulation results show that the proposed EBP method has significant advantage over the comparing methods in terms of MSPE and coverage probability and length of the resulting prediction interval. A real-data example from agricultural-animal genetics is discussed.

papers.title: Distributional change point analysis: high dimensionality, nonstationary dependence, and computational constraints
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22422v1

summary.one_liner: A method for detecting and locating distributional change points in high-dimensional, nonstationary time series, using sparse random projections of characteristic functions and a Gaussian multiplier bootstrap for inference.
summary.plain: The paper addresses a common problem: spotting the moments when the overall pattern of a long, many-variable data stream shifts, such as when the way neurons fire changes. The authors propose a procedure that compresses the many variables into a small number of random summaries, which keeps computation cheap and limits noise from irrelevant variables. They report theoretical guarantees on false alarms and on how precisely change times are located, and show simulations and an application to neural recordings.
summary.why:
Many real data streams have dozens or hundreds of variables and dependence that changes over time, which breaks many standard change detection tools. The paper's main claims are theoretical guarantees under these conditions, plus a Gaussian approximation result for high-dimensional sparse time series that the authors say is of independent interest. The text alone does not show how it compares with existing methods in practice, so its practical reach is uncertain.</research-level>
<parameter name="background">- Change point: a time at which the statistical behavior of a data sequence changes.
- Distribution: the full pattern of how likely each value is, which is broader than just the average.
- Characteristic function: a mathematical fingerprint of a distribution, used here to compare distributions via a set of numbers.
- High-dimensional: many variables measured at once, so the number of variables may be large relative to the sample.
- Random projection: multiplying data by random weights to compress many variables into fewer summaries.
- Nonstationary dependence: the way observations relate to their neighbors in time changes over time.
- Gaussian multiplier bootstrap: a resampling technique that uses random normal weights to approximate the distribution of a test statistic, giving thresholds for false alarms.
- Asymptotic: describes behavior as the amount of data grows large.

papers.abstract: We study general distributional change point analysis for high-dimensional time series under nonstationary temporal dependence and limited computational resources. To mitigate noise accumulation from irrelevant coordinates and reduce the computational cost, we propose a sparse random projection procedure based on characteristic functions. We quantify the computational complexity of the random projections and show that the required number of projections grows polynomially with the ambient dimension. To accommodate nonstationary temporal dependence, a Gaussian multiplier bootstrap based on contrasts of local empirical characteristic functions is developed. We establish asymptotic false detection control and simultaneous guarantees for estimating the number and locations of multiple change points, with a near-parametric uniform localization rate up to logarithmic factors. A key technical innovation is a Gaussian approximation for high-dimensional multi-scale sparse time series, which is of independent interest. Simulation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed procedure in detecting and localizing distributional changes under various temporal dependence structures. An application to neural recordings further illustrates the practical utility of the proposed method in detecting diverse distributional changes in neural activity.

papers.title: tsspiral: An R Package to Create Circular Versions of Time Series Plots
papers.label: arXiv:2611.21327v1

summary.background:
- A time series is a sequence of values recorded at regular times, such as daily or monthly readings.
- Seasonality means a pattern that repeats on a fixed cycle, such as every year.
- Polar coordinates locate points by distance from a centre and an angle, instead of by x and y positions.
- R is a programming language widely used for statistics; ggplot2 is a plotting package for R built on a "grammar of graphics", a system for building charts from layered parts.
- A spiral plot here means a circular plot in which successive years stack outward as concentric rings.
summary.one_liner: tsspiral is an open-source R package that adds polar-coordinate "spiral" plots for time series to the ggplot2 grammar of graphics, with each year drawn as a ring and day of year as angle.
summary.plain: Time series are measurements taken over time, such as daily temperatures or sales. This paper presents a software tool that draws these measurements around circles, so each year becomes a ring and the position within the year becomes the angle, like the face of a clock. The authors say this makes repeating yearly or seasonal patterns easier to spot, especially in long records.
summary.why: Long records with repeating cycles are common in many fields, and a plot that shows those cycles clearly can help analysts and communicators. The text presents this as a practical tool rather than a new finding, and it does not report any tests showing it works better than standard plots.

papers.abstract: `tsspiral` is an open-source R package that introduces a circular approach to time series visualisation using polar coordinates. We refer to this circular representation of time series data as a spiral. `tsspiral` provides a collection of `ggplot2` geometries for creating a spiral representation of time series data. In our approach, we arrange observations around a circle. Each year is represented by a circle, with the angular position corresponding to the day of the year, and successive years appear as concentric rings. This arrangement facilitates the exploration of periodicity, seasonality, and recurring temporal patterns, particularly in long time series. The package also supports temporal hierarchical visualisations to compare patterns across time scales. By bringing polar-coordinate-based visualisation into routine time series analysis, `tsspiral` offers a practical tool for exploring temporal patterns and communicating complex time-dependent structures. Rather than treating spiral plots as standalone graphics, our approach brings them into the grammar of graphics framework, enabling users to explore temporal patterns through a broader range of visual encodings.

papers.title: A δ-adjusted Method for Tipping Point Sensitivity Analysis for a Binary Outcome with Missing Values
papers.label: arXiv:2611.21939v1

summary.background:
- Missing data: outcomes not observed for some trial participants, for example after they drop out.
- Sensitivity analysis: re-running the analysis under alternative assumptions about the missing values to see whether conclusions hold.
- Delta-adjustment: adding a fixed sensitivity value to the imputed (filled-in) outcomes for one or both treatment groups, representing how much worse or better missing participants might have fared.
- Tipping point: the smallest such adjustment at which a statistically significant result stops being significant.
- Binary outcome: a result with only two possible values, such as success or failure.
- Logit: a mathematical transformation that maps probabilities (between 0 and 1) onto an unbounded scale, where the sensitivity shift is applied.
- Composite endpoint: a single outcome that counts several different events together as one.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes a delta-adjusted tipping point sensitivity analysis for binary outcomes with missing data, by adding a shift on the logit scale to the estimated response probability, and applies it to a tirzepatide clinical trial with a composite binary endpoint.
summary.plain: Clinical trials often lose some participants' results partway through, and statisticians need to check whether the conclusion would change if the missing results were different from what was assumed. This paper offers such a check for yes/no outcomes (such as whether a patient met a combined health goal), where earlier versions of the check existed only for measured numbers. The authors apply the method to a trial comparing two doses of tirzepatide, a diabetes and weight-loss drug.
summary.why: Missing data can change trial conclusions, so a standard way to test how fragile a result is matters for regulatory and clinical decisions. The text suggests the method is meant for broad use in trials with binary endpoints, but its practical value beyond this example is not shown in the text provided.

papers.abstract: Missing data remain a persistent challenge in clinical trials despite preventive efforts. Handling missing data in clinical trials requires not only a primary analysis but also sensitivity analyses, as the underlying missingness assumptions are difficult to verify. The δ-adjusted analysis, which assesses the robustness of primary results by adding a sensitivity parameter δ for one or both treatment groups, has been widely used for continuous outcomes. Then, a set of tipping points which flip the significance of the primary analysis can be identified. However, there is no corresponding δ-adjusted method for binary variables. In this article, we propose a δ-adjusted method for binary variables that addresses this gap. This method assesses robustness by adding a sensitivity parameter to the logit function of the estimated response probability under the primary imputation approach and shares the same property as the δ-adjusted method for continuous variables. We applied this method to a clinical trial evaluating the treatment effect of tirzepatide 15 mg versus 5 mg on a composite binary endpoint. This method provides a principled sensitivity analysis framework for binary endpoints with broad applicability in clinical trials.
